# The Factory Pattern Story

### From One Chat Service to Simple Factory, Registry & Abstract Factory

> **LLD Trainer Tutorial** · Java + Python
>
> Understand **Dependency Inversion**, **Simple Factory**, **Registry-based Factory**, the **Open/Closed Principle**, and **Abstract Factory** by living through the problems that created them.

---

## 🎨 How to Read the Pictures

Every picture in this tutorial uses the **same colors for the same roles**. Learn them once and every picture reads itself. Each chapter picture also has a **How it works** panel on the right: read the numbered steps while following the arrows.

| Color | Role |
|---|---|
| 🟦 **Blue** | Your service or client code |
| 🟪 **Purple** | An interface, the contract everyone agrees on |
| 🟧 **Orange** | A factory, the place where objects are created |
| 🟩 **Green** | A concrete class that does the real work |
| 🟢 **Teal** | A registry, a lookup table of creators |
| 🟥 **Red** | A problem or pain point |
| **Light blue / Pink** | OpenAI products / Anthropic products |

## 🎬 Meet the Cast

> **You** are **Priya**, a backend engineer at a startup called **AskBot**. AskBot is an app that sits on top of large language models (LLMs) and answers customer questions.
>
> **Rahul** is your manager. He is friendly, but his requirements change every few weeks.
>
> **The codebase** starts small. By the end of this story, it has around **100 services** that need an LLM.

# Chapter 1 — Day One: "Just Use OpenAI"

> 📅 **Monday morning.** Rahul drops by Priya's desk.
>
> **Rahul:** "We're launching AskBot next week. Build a `ChatService` that sends the user's question to OpenAI and returns the answer. Keep it simple."
>
> Priya writes the most natural code possible.

![Chapter 1: ChatService creates OpenAIClient directly](data:image/png;base64,)

### Java

```java
class OpenAIClient {

    public String chat(String prompt) {
        return "Response from OpenAI";
    }
}

class ChatService {

    private OpenAIClient client;

    public ChatService() {
        client = new OpenAIClient();   // ChatService builds its own client
    }

    public String chat(String prompt) {
        return client.chat(prompt);
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ChatService service = new ChatService();
        System.out.println(service.chat("Explain Factory Pattern"));
    }
}
```

### Python

```python
class OpenAIClient:

    def chat(self, prompt):
        return "Response from OpenAI"

class ChatService:

    def __init__(self):
        self.client = OpenAIClient()   # ChatService builds its own client

    def chat(self, prompt):
        return self.client.chat(prompt)

service = ChatService()
print(service.chat("Explain Factory Pattern"))
```

> ✅ **Is anything wrong here?** Not yet. When the requirement is "we only use OpenAI", this code is fine. Good design isn't about predicting every future. It's about reacting well when the future arrives.

**Now look closely at one detail:** the arrow says `new OpenAIClient()`. `ChatService` doesn't just *use* OpenAI. It **builds** OpenAI itself. Remember this, because it's about to hurt.

---

# Chapter 2 — One Month Later: "We're Switching to Anthropic"

> 📅 **A month later.** A Slack message pops up.
>
> **Rahul:** "Finance compared prices. We're moving from OpenAI to Anthropic. Can you switch it today?"
>
> Priya opens `ChatService`, the heart of the product, and starts editing.

```java
class ChatService {

    private AnthropicClient client;         // changed

    public ChatService() {
        client = new AnthropicClient();     // changed
    }
}
```

![Chapter 2: switching vendor forces edits to ChatService](data:image/png;base64,)

### 🚨 The first design smell

Ask yourself: **why did a pricing decision force Priya to edit the core business class?**

Because the **high-level** class (`ChatService`, which holds the business logic) knows the exact name of a **low-level** detail (`OpenAIClient`, a vendor SDK wrapper).

> 🔌 **Analogy: the wall socket.**
> Your laptop charger plugs into a wall socket. It doesn't care whether the power comes from a coal plant, a solar farm, or a dam. If you had to **rewire your laptop** every time the city changed power plants, that would be absurd.
>
> Right now, `ChatService` is a laptop that has been **soldered directly to one power plant**.

---

# Chapter 3 — The Fix: Dependency Inversion

Priya asks the key question:

> **"Why should `ChatService` care whether the provider is OpenAI or Anthropic?"**

It shouldn't. All it needs is *something that can chat*. So she defines that "something" as a contract, the **socket**.

![Chapter 3: ChatService depends on the LLMClient interface](data:image/png;base64,)

> 🔁 **Why is it called "inversion"?** Look at the arrows. Before, `ChatService` pointed **down** at `OpenAIClient`. Now **both** point **toward the interface in the middle**. The vendor classes now depend on a contract that the business side owns. The dependency direction has been flipped.

### Java

```java
interface LLMClient {
    String chat(String prompt);
}

class OpenAIClient implements LLMClient {
    @Override
    public String chat(String prompt) {
        return "Response from OpenAI";
    }
}

class AnthropicClient implements LLMClient {
    @Override
    public String chat(String prompt) {
        return "Response from Anthropic";
    }
}

class ChatService {

    private final LLMClient client;

    public ChatService(LLMClient client) {   // the client is handed in from outside
        this.client = client;
    }

    public String chat(String prompt) {
        return client.chat(prompt);
    }
}
```

Usage. Swap providers **without touching `ChatService`**:

```java
ChatService service = new ChatService(new OpenAIClient());
System.out.println(service.chat("Explain Factory Pattern"));

ChatService service2 = new ChatService(new AnthropicClient());   // ChatService unchanged
```

### Python

Python doesn't need a formal interface, but an abstract base class states the contract clearly.

```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class LLMClient(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    def chat(self, prompt):
        pass

class OpenAIClient(LLMClient):

    def chat(self, prompt):
        return "Response from OpenAI"

class AnthropicClient(LLMClient):

    def chat(self, prompt):
        return "Response from Anthropic"

class ChatService:

    def __init__(self, client: LLMClient):
        self.client = client

    def chat(self, prompt):
        return self.client.chat(prompt)

service = ChatService(OpenAIClient())
print(service.chat("Explain Factory Pattern"))

service = ChatService(AnthropicClient())   # ChatService unchanged
```

### 📌 What did we just learn? Two ideas, not one

| Idea | Meaning in this story |
|---|---|
| **Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)** | `ChatService` depends on the `LLMClient` **abstraction**, not on a concrete vendor. |
| **Dependency Injection (DI)** | The client is **handed in** through the constructor instead of being built inside. |

> 😌 **Priya's relief:** next time Rahul changes vendors, `ChatService` doesn't change at all.

---

# Chapter 4 — Three Providers, and `if/else` Starts Spreading

> 📅 **A few months later.**
>
> **Rahul:** "Big enterprise customers want a choice. Support **OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini**. The customer's config file decides which one."
>
> The provider is now a **string** that arrives at runtime, like `"openai"`. Someone has to turn that string into an object. Priya takes the quickest route and puts it inside `ChatService`.

### Java

```java
class ChatService {

    private LLMClient client;

    public ChatService(String provider) {
        if (provider.equals("openai")) {
            client = new OpenAIClient();
        } else if (provider.equals("anthropic")) {
            client = new AnthropicClient();
        } else if (provider.equals("gemini")) {
            client = new GeminiClient();
        }
    }

    public String chat(String prompt) {
        return client.chat(prompt);
    }
}
```

### Python

```python
class ChatService:

    def __init__(self, provider):
        if provider == "openai":
            self.client = OpenAIClient()
        elif provider == "anthropic":
            self.client = AnthropicClient()
        elif provider == "gemini":
            self.client = GeminiClient()

    def chat(self, prompt):
        return self.client.chat(prompt)
```

### 🚨 Now zoom out to the whole company

AskBot grows. The **SummaryService**, **TranslationService**, **SupportBotService**, and eventually around 100 services all need an LLM. And every team copies the same `if/else`.

![Chapter 4: every service copies the same if/else](data:image/png;base64,)

> 😫 **The nightmare:** Rahul says "add Mistral". Priya now has to find and edit **100 copies** of the same `if/else`. She misses one, and it breaks in production at 2 a.m.

### What went wrong?

`ChatService` was supposed to handle **chat logic**. Now it also knows **how to build every provider**. That's a second job, the **creation** job. When the same creation job is copied into 100 classes, every new provider means 100 edits.

> 🧩 **Principles being broken:**
> - **Single Responsibility (SRP):** services now do chatting **and** constructing.
> - **Open/Closed (OCP):** adding a provider means modifying many existing, working classes.

---

# Chapter 5 — Simple Factory: "Build It in One Place"

Priya's goal is simple:

> **Move all object creation into ONE place. Every service just asks that place.**

> 🍝 **Analogy: the restaurant kitchen.**
> At a restaurant, you say "one pasta, please". You don't walk into the kitchen and cook it yourself. The **kitchen** knows the recipe. You only know the **menu name**.
>
> The factory is the kitchen. `"openai"` is the menu name. The object is your plate.

![Chapter 5: Simple Factory centralizes creation](data:image/png;base64,)

### Java

```java
class LLMClientFactory {

    public static LLMClient create(String provider) {

        if (provider.equals("openai")) {
            return new OpenAIClient();
        }
        if (provider.equals("anthropic")) {
            return new AnthropicClient();
        }
        if (provider.equals("gemini")) {
            return new GeminiClient();
        }

        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown provider: " + provider);
    }
}

class ChatService {

    private final LLMClient client;

    public ChatService(String provider) {
        this.client = LLMClientFactory.create(provider);   // just ask the kitchen
    }

    public String chat(String prompt) {
        return client.chat(prompt);
    }
}
```

```java
ChatService service = new ChatService("openai");
System.out.println(service.chat("Explain Factory Pattern"));
```

### Python

```python
class LLMClientFactory:

    @staticmethod
    def create(provider):
        if provider == "openai":
            return OpenAIClient()
        if provider == "anthropic":
            return AnthropicClient()
        if provider == "gemini":
            return GeminiClient()

        raise ValueError(f"Unknown provider: {provider}")

class ChatService:

    def __init__(self, provider):
        self.client = LLMClientFactory.create(provider)

    def chat(self, prompt):
        return self.client.chat(prompt)

service = ChatService("openai")
print(service.chat("Explain Factory Pattern"))
```

### 🎞️ Watch one request, step by step

```mermaid

    participant F as LLMClientFactory
    participant O as OpenAIClient

    F-->>C: returns it as an LLMClient
```

> 👀 **Notice:** `ChatService` never writes `new OpenAIClient()`. It never even says "OpenAI" as a class name. It only knows the menu name `"openai"` and the `LLMClient` contract.

### Before vs. after

| | Before (Chapter 4) | After (Simple Factory) |
|---|---|---|
| Where is creation logic? | Copied into ~100 services | In **one** factory |
| Adding Mistral means... | Editing ~100 files | Editing **1** file |
| Services know vendor classes? | Yes | No, only a name string |

# Chapter 6 — Honesty Check: The Factory Keeps Growing

> 📅 **Six months later.**
>
> **Rahul:** "Add Mistral. Oh, and Cohere. And DeepSeek. And..."

Priya opens the factory. It now looks like this:

```java
if (provider.equals("openai"))    { ... }
if (provider.equals("anthropic")) { ... }
if (provider.equals("gemini"))    { ... }
if (provider.equals("mistral"))   { ... }
if (provider.equals("cohere"))    { ... }
if (provider.equals("deepseek"))  { ... }
// ... 44 more
```

![Chapter 6: the conditional factory must be edited for every provider](data:image/png;base64,)

### ❓ Does Simple Factory fully satisfy the Open/Closed Principle?

**No.** This is an important point to be honest about.

- Every new provider still means **modifying** the factory.
- So the conditional factory is **not closed for modification**.

**But** it was still a big win. We moved the modification point from ~100 places to **1 place**. That's practical progress, not perfection.

> 🎯 **Question to ask the class:** "Every time we add a provider, should we have to open this file?"

---

# Chapter 7 — Registry Factory: "Look It Up, Don't Branch"

Priya changes her thinking:

> Instead of **writing a branch** for every provider, keep a **lookup table** that maps each name to a creator.

> 📇 **Analogy: your phone's contact list.**
> Your phone doesn't contain an `if` statement for each friend. It has a **list**: name → number. A new friend? You **add a contact**. You don't rebuild the phone.

![Chapter 7: Registry Factory looks up creators by name](data:image/png;base64,)

### Java — Step 1: a registry filled in one place

Java's `Supplier<T>` means "a function that takes nothing and returns a `T`". A constructor reference like `OpenAIClient::new` fits perfectly.

```java
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

class LLMClientFactory {

    private static final Map<String, Supplier<LLMClient>> registry = new HashMap<>();

    static {
        registry.put("openai",    OpenAIClient::new);
        registry.put("anthropic", AnthropicClient::new);
        registry.put("gemini",    GeminiClient::new);
    }

    public static LLMClient create(String provider) {
        Supplier<LLMClient> creator = registry.get(provider);
        if (creator == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown provider: " + provider);
        }
        return creator.get();   // NOW the object is actually built
    }
}
```

> 💡 **`OpenAIClient::new` does not create an object.** It's like writing down a recipe. `creator.get()` is when the cooking actually happens.

### Java — Step 2: explicit registration (the factory never changes again)

The `static` block still lives inside the factory. Let's move registration **outside** it.

```java
class LLMClientFactory {

    private static final Map<String, Supplier<LLMClient>> registry = new HashMap<>();

    public static void register(String provider, Supplier<LLMClient> creator) {
        registry.put(provider, creator);
    }

    public static LLMClient create(String provider) {
        Supplier<LLMClient> creator = registry.get(provider);
        if (creator == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown provider: " + provider);
        }
        return creator.get();
    }
}
```

```java
// App startup (or each provider's own module)
LLMClientFactory.register("openai",    OpenAIClient::new);
LLMClientFactory.register("anthropic", AnthropicClient::new);
LLMClientFactory.register("mistral",   MistralClient::new);   // new provider, factory untouched

// Anywhere in the app
LLMClient client = LLMClientFactory.create("openai");
```

### Python

A Python class is already callable, so the class itself works as the creator.

```python
class LLMClientFactory:

    _registry = {}

    @classmethod
    def register(cls, provider, creator):
        cls._registry[provider] = creator

    @classmethod
    def create(cls, provider):
        creator = cls._registry.get(provider)
        if creator is None:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown provider: {provider}")
        return creator()

LLMClientFactory.register("openai", OpenAIClient)
LLMClientFactory.register("anthropic", AnthropicClient)
LLMClientFactory.register("gemini", GeminiClient)

client = LLMClientFactory.create("openai")
```

> 🐍 **Python bonus:** a decorator lets each class register itself right where it's defined.
>
> ```python
> def register_provider(name):
>     def wrapper(cls):
>         LLMClientFactory.register(name, cls)
>         return cls
>     return wrapper
>
>
> @register_provider("mistral")
> class MistralClient(LLMClient):
>     def chat(self, prompt):
>         return "Response from Mistral"
> ```

> ⚠️ **Watch out:** if `create("mistral")` runs **before** `register("mistral", ...)`, it fails at runtime. Registration must happen at startup.

# Chapter 8 — Plot Twist: The App Needs a *Family* of Objects

> 📅 **Next quarter.**
>
> **Rahul:** "Customers complain AskBot doesn't know **their** documents. Make it answer using their company data."
>
> Priya explains that this needs **RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation**.

### How RAG works, in pictures

![Chapter 8: the RAG flow needs a ChatClient and a VectorClient](data:image/png;base64,)

An **embedding** (or vector) is a list of numbers that captures the *meaning* of text. Texts with similar meaning get similar numbers, so the database can find relevant documents.

### 🎯 The big change

Before, **one provider = one object**. Now, **one provider = a family of objects**.

> 🔌 **Analogy: phone charger and cable.**
> A brand's charger and its cable are designed to work together. Mix a random cable with a random charger and it might charge slowly, or not at all. You want **a matched set**.

### 🚨 The danger: mixed families

Embeddings from different providers aren't compatible. If documents were stored using one provider's embeddings and the question is embedded with another's, the numbers don't line up, and search quietly returns garbage. **No error. Just wrong answers.**

![Chapter 8: matched vs mixed families](data:image/png;base64,)

> 📝 **Real-world note:** in practice, Anthropic doesn't offer its own embedding model and points developers to partners such as Voyage AI. That actually makes the pattern *more* useful: an `AnthropicFactory` could return an `AnthropicChatClient` plus a `VoyageVectorClient`. The client code never needs to know. We keep `AnthropicVectorClient` here to keep the example simple.

### Product interfaces

**Java**

```java
interface ChatClient {
    String chat(String prompt);
}

interface VectorClient {
    double[] embed(String text);
}

class OpenAIChatClient implements ChatClient {
    @Override
    public String chat(String prompt) { return "OpenAI response"; }
}

class OpenAIVectorClient implements VectorClient {
    @Override
    public double[] embed(String text) { return new double[]{0.1, 0.2, 0.3}; }
}

class AnthropicChatClient implements ChatClient {
    @Override
    public String chat(String prompt) { return "Anthropic response"; }
}

class AnthropicVectorClient implements VectorClient {
    @Override
    public double[] embed(String text) { return new double[]{0.4, 0.5, 0.6}; }
}
```

### Why Simple Factory now feels awkward

We *could* stretch the old factory:

```text
create("openai-chat")
create("openai-vector")
create("anthropic-chat")
create("anthropic-vector")
```

But then **nothing stops** a service from calling `create("openai-chat")` and `create("anthropic-vector")`. The factory would have to understand combinations, and the family rule would live only in people's heads.

What we really want to say is:

> **"Give me the OpenAI factory." Then everything it makes is guaranteed to be OpenAI.**

---

# Chapter 9 — Abstract Factory: "One Factory per Family"

> 🪑 **Analogy: furniture showrooms.**
> A "Modern" showroom sells a modern chair, a modern sofa, and a modern table. A "Victorian" showroom sells the Victorian versions. Pick **one showroom**, and everything you buy matches automatically.

![Chapter 9: Abstract Factory creates a family per provider](data:image/png;base64,)

> **A concrete factory creates a whole family of related products, and only that family.**

### Java

```java
interface AIClientFactory {
    ChatClient createChatClient();
    VectorClient createVectorClient();
}

class OpenAIFactory implements AIClientFactory {
    @Override
    public ChatClient createChatClient()     { return new OpenAIChatClient(); }
    @Override
    public VectorClient createVectorClient() { return new OpenAIVectorClient(); }
}

class AnthropicFactory implements AIClientFactory {
    @Override
    public ChatClient createChatClient()     { return new AnthropicChatClient(); }
    @Override
    public VectorClient createVectorClient() { return new AnthropicVectorClient(); }
}
```

The client receives **one factory** and gets a matched family from it:

```java
class ChatService {

    private final ChatClient chatClient;
    private final VectorClient vectorClient;

    public ChatService(AIClientFactory factory) {
        this.chatClient   = factory.createChatClient();
        this.vectorClient = factory.createVectorClient();
    }

    public String chat(String prompt) {
        double[] vector = vectorClient.embed(prompt);
        // Simplified: normally the vector is used to fetch
        // relevant documents from a vector database.
        return chatClient.chat(prompt);
    }
}
```

```java
ChatService service = new ChatService(new OpenAIFactory());

ChatService service2 = new ChatService(new AnthropicFactory());   // ChatService unchanged
```

### Python

```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class AIClientFactory(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    def create_chat_client(self):
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def create_vector_client(self):
        pass

class OpenAIFactory(AIClientFactory):

    def create_chat_client(self):
        return OpenAIChatClient()

    def create_vector_client(self):
        return OpenAIVectorClient()

class AnthropicFactory(AIClientFactory):

    def create_chat_client(self):
        return AnthropicChatClient()

    def create_vector_client(self):
        return AnthropicVectorClient()

class ChatService:

    def __init__(self, factory: AIClientFactory):
        self.chat_client = factory.create_chat_client()
        self.vector_client = factory.create_vector_client()

    def chat(self, prompt):
        vector = self.vector_client.embed(prompt)
        # Simplified: normally used to fetch relevant documents.
        return self.chat_client.chat(prompt)

service = ChatService(OpenAIFactory())
service = ChatService(AnthropicFactory())   # ChatService unchanged
```

### Simple Factory vs. Abstract Factory, side by side

![Simple Factory vs Abstract Factory](data:image/png;base64,)

| | Simple Factory | Abstract Factory |
|---|---|---|
| Question it answers | "Which **object**?" | "Which **family** of objects?" |
| Output | One product | Several related products |
| Guarantees matching? | No | **Yes** |

# Chapter 10 — The Finale: Registry + Abstract Factory Together

> 📅 **Final requirement.**
>
> **Rahul:** "Each customer's config says `provider: openai` or `provider: anthropic`. Pick the right family at runtime."
>
> The provider is a **string** again. Priya reuses the Registry idea, but now the registry stores **factories** instead of single clients.

![Chapter 10: registry picks the factory, factory builds the family](data:image/png;base64,)

*Solid arrows show the path that is chosen. Dashed gray arrows show the path that is available but not chosen.*

### Java

```java
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

class AIFactoryRegistry {

    private static final Map<String, Supplier<AIClientFactory>> registry = new HashMap<>();

    public static void register(String provider, Supplier<AIClientFactory> creator) {
        registry.put(provider, creator);
    }

    public static AIClientFactory get(String provider) {
        Supplier<AIClientFactory> creator = registry.get(provider);
        if (creator == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown provider: " + provider);
        }
        return creator.get();
    }
}
```

```java
// Startup
AIFactoryRegistry.register("openai",    OpenAIFactory::new);
AIFactoryRegistry.register("anthropic", AnthropicFactory::new);

// Runtime
String provider = config.get("provider");                 // e.g. "openai"
AIClientFactory factory = AIFactoryRegistry.get(provider);
ChatService service = new ChatService(factory);
```

### Python

```python
class AIFactoryRegistry:

    _registry = {}

    @classmethod
    def register(cls, provider, factory_cls):
        cls._registry[provider] = factory_cls

    @classmethod
    def get(cls, provider):
        factory_cls = cls._registry.get(provider)
        if factory_cls is None:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown provider: {provider}")
        return factory_cls()

AIFactoryRegistry.register("openai", OpenAIFactory)
AIFactoryRegistry.register("anthropic", AnthropicFactory)

factory = AIFactoryRegistry.get("openai")
service = ChatService(factory)
```

> 🏁 **End of the story.** Adding a brand-new provider family now means writing its product classes and one factory, then calling `register(...)` once. **Nothing that already works is edited.**

---

# 🧠 Clearing Up Common Confusions

### Factory vs. Dependency Injection

They answer **different questions** and work best **together**.

| | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Dependency Injection** | "How does my object **receive** its dependency?" | `new ChatService(client)` |
| **Factory** | "How do I **create** the right implementation?" | `LLMClientFactory.create("openai")` |

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontSize':'15px', 'fontFamily':'Arial', 'lineColor':'#475569', 'edgeLabelBackground':'#FFFFFF'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    F["Factory"] -->|"creates"| C["LLMClient"]
    C -->|"injected into"| S["ChatService"]

    classDef factory fill:#D97706,stroke:#78350F,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFFFFF
    classDef iface fill:#7C3AED,stroke:#4C1D95,stroke-width:3px,color:#FFFFFF
    classDef service fill:#1D4ED8,stroke:#1E3A8A,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFFFFF

    class F factory
    class C iface
    class S service
```

### Factory vs. Strategy

| | Concerned with | Mental model |
|---|---|---|
| **Factory** | Object **creation** | "Which **object**?" |
| **Strategy** | Swappable **behavior** | "Which **behavior**?" |

They often appear together. A factory **creates** `OpenAIChatClient`, and that object then **provides** the chat behavior (the strategy).

### Factory and A/B experiments

Suppose AskBot tests two recommendation engines.

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontSize':'15px', 'fontFamily':'Arial', 'lineColor':'#475569', 'edgeLabelBackground':'#FFFFFF'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    U["User"] --> EX["Experiment Service"]
    EX -->|"variant = B"| F["Engine Factory"]
    F -.->|"A"| EA["Engine A"]
    F -->|"B"| EB["Engine B"]

    classDef io fill:#E2E8F0,stroke:#475569,stroke-width:2px,color:#0F172A
    classDef service fill:#1D4ED8,stroke:#1E3A8A,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFFFFF
    classDef factory fill:#D97706,stroke:#78350F,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFFFFF
    classDef chosen fill:#059669,stroke:#064E3B,stroke-width:3px,color:#FFFFFF
    classDef idle fill:#CBD5E1,stroke:#64748B,stroke-width:2px,color:#334155

    class U io
    class EX service
    class F factory
    class EB chosen
    class EA idle
```

- The **experiment** decides *which variant* this user gets.
- The **factory** decides *which implementation* to create for that variant.

> ⚠️ A/B testing doesn't *require* a Factory. A factory helps when each variant maps to a **different implementation** that must be created at runtime.

# 🧭 The Whole Story in One Table

| Chapter | 🟥 Pain | 🟩 Fix | Principle / Pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Vendor change forces edits to core code | Depend on an interface | **DIP** + **DI** |
| 4 | `if/else` copied into ~100 services | Create in one place | **Simple Factory** |
| 6 | Factory must be edited for every provider | Lookup table of creators | **Registry Factory** (OCP) |
| 8 | Products must come as a matched set | One factory per family | **Abstract Factory** |
| 10 | Family must be chosen at runtime | Registry of factories | **Registry + Abstract Factory** |

# 🎓 The Final Mental Model: Four Questions

| Ask yourself... | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. What does my high-level class depend on? | An **abstraction** (DIP) |
| 2. Where should object creation happen? | In a **Factory** |
| 3. How do I avoid editing a huge conditional factory? | A **Registry** |
| 4. What if one provider gives several related products? | An **Abstract Factory** |

### Memory trick

| Concept | One-line question |
|---|---|
| **Factory** | "Which **OBJECT**?" |
| **Abstract Factory** | "Which **FAMILY** of objects?" |
| **Registry** | "Which **CREATOR** is registered?" |
| **Dependency Injection** | "How does my object **RECEIVE** its dependency?" |

---

# 🙋 Classroom Questions

<details>
<summary><b>Q1. Why shouldn't <code>ChatService</code> directly create <code>OpenAIClient</code>?</b></summary>

Because `ChatService` should depend on an abstraction (`LLMClient`), not on a concrete vendor. Otherwise every vendor change forces edits to core business code.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Q2. Why not put provider selection inside every client?</b></summary>

It duplicates creation logic across many classes. Adding one provider then means editing all of them, and it's easy to miss one.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Q3. What does Simple Factory centralize?</b></summary>

Object creation. The "which class do I build?" decision now lives in one place.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Q4. Does Simple Factory completely satisfy OCP?</b></summary>

Not necessarily. A conditional factory still has to be modified whenever a new provider is added. It reduces the number of places to modify from many to one.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Q5. How can we avoid modifying the factory for every new provider?</b></summary>

Use a registry-based factory. New providers are added through `register(...)` calls, and the factory class stays unchanged.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Q6. When does Abstract Factory become useful?</b></summary>

When you need to create **families of related objects** that must match, such as a chat client and a vector client from the same provider.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Q7. In one line, how is Simple Factory different from Abstract Factory?</b></summary>

Simple Factory: one factory produces **one product**. Abstract Factory: each concrete factory produces a **family of products**.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Q8. How are Factory and Dependency Injection related?</b></summary>

Factory **creates** the dependency; DI **delivers** it to the class that needs it. They're commonly used together.
</details>

---

# 📋 Interview Summary

| Pattern | One-line definition | Flow |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple Factory** | Centralizes creation of objects based on some input. | input → factory → object |
| **Registry Factory** | Uses a registry of creators so new implementations can be added without new conditional branches. | input → registry → creator → object |
| **Abstract Factory** | Provides an interface for creating families of related objects. | factory → product A + product B |

---

# 👩‍🏫 Trainer Notes: Teaching This as a Story

Don't open with "Today we're learning the Factory Pattern." Open with a problem, and let students **discover** each pattern.

| Story beat | Ask the class | Students discover |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "The manager wants Anthropic instead of OpenAI. What must change?" | The direct dependency problem, leading to **DIP** |
| 2 | "We now support three providers. Where should creation happen?" | Creation is a separate responsibility |
| 3 | "What if 100 services need the same selection?" | **Simple Factory** |
| 4 | "What happens when the factory has 50 providers?" | **Registry** |
| 5 | "Every provider now gives chat **and** vector clients. Can the simple factory keep them matched?" | **Abstract Factory** |

> 🎯 **Don't memorize the pattern first. Understand the problem that forced the pattern to appear.**
